title: Round holes on the Moon
teaches: Why craters were long thought to be volcanoes, how a fast impact becomes an explosion, and how geologists trained the Apollo crews

blocks.text: In the autumn of 1891 Grove Karl Gilbert, chief geologist of the US Geological Survey, borrowed time on the large refracting telescope at the Naval Observatory in Washington and spent eighteen nights drawing the Moon. Most astronomers of his day took the Moon's craters to be volcanoes. They were round, they were everywhere, and many had a peak in the middle, which looked like the cone at the centre of a volcanic crater on Earth.

Gilbert thought the comparison failed on every measurement he could make. Volcanic craters on Earth sit on top of mountains; the Moon's craters are holes whose floors lie below the surrounding plain. Large lunar craters are tens or hundreds of kilometres across, far wider than any volcanic crater known. Their central peaks are low, and they rarely have a crater of their own at the top. In 1893 he published *The Moon's Face*, arguing that the craters had been punched by solid bodies falling onto the surface.

blocks.caption: Round craters on the far side of the Moon, photographed from orbit. Almost every one of them is circular.

blocks.text: He could not answer one objection, and he raised it himself. Things falling onto the Moon from space should arrive at every angle, and most of them at a slant: the single most likely angle is 45°, and a vertical hit is rare. Throw a stone into wet sand at a slant and it leaves an oval scoop, longer along the direction it was travelling. Yet almost every crater on the Moon is round. His best answer was that the Moon had grown from a ring of small bodies circling the Earth, whose last stragglers would have struck it nearly head-on. Few people found that convincing, and the volcanic view held for another half century.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Lunar craters are holes with floors below the surrounding plain, unlike volcanic craters, which sit on mountains.
Gilbert argued in 1893 that impacts made them, but could not explain why craters from slanting impacts would be round.

blocks.text: The same year Gilbert went to see a crater on Earth: a bowl about 1.2 kilometres across and 170 metres deep in the desert of northern Arizona, now called Meteor Crater. Thousands of pieces of iron meteorite lay scattered around it. Gilbert reasoned that if a huge iron body had made the hole, it should still be buried underneath. A survey with a sensitive compass needle found no pull from a large buried mass of iron, and he calculated that the rock piled in the rim had about the same volume as the hole, leaving no room for a buried mass. He concluded that a steam explosion, driven by volcanic heat underground, had blown the crater out.

blocks.caption: Meteor Crater, Arizona, about 1.2 km across. It formed about 50,000 years ago.

blocks.text: A Philadelphia mining engineer, Daniel Barringer, disagreed and bought the land in 1903, sure that millions of tonnes of iron lay below. His company drilled for 26 years and found broken rock and small grains of meteoritic iron, but never the great mass. Barringer was right that an impact made the crater, and wrong that the iron body would still be lying under it. As later work showed, an object arriving at many kilometres a second does not survive its landing.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Gilbert judged Meteor Crater a steam explosion, partly because no buried iron mass could be found.
Barringer drilled for the iron for 26 years; it had been vaporized and scattered when it hit.

blocks.text: The answer to both puzzles is speed. Bodies arriving from space hit the Moon at 10 to 30 kilometres a second, ten to thirty times faster than a rifle bullet. In 1916 the Estonian astronomer Ernst Öpik, and in 1924 the New Zealand astronomer Algernon Gifford, worked out what that implies. At such a speed the object carries more energy, kilogram for kilogram, than the same mass of high explosive. It drives only about its own width into the ground before the rock in front of it, crushed by the collision, brings it to a halt within a fraction of a second, and its energy goes into a **shock wave**: a pulse of extreme pressure that spreads through the rock in every direction from the point of impact, melting and vaporizing the object and much of the rock around it.

Because the energy is released at nearly a single point below the surface, what the slant of the arrival mostly decides is where the **ejecta**, the debris thrown out of the crater, lands, not the shape of the hole. The crater comes out round, just as a buried charge of explosive leaves a round crater however the charge was carried in. Only very low, grazing impacts, below about 15°, leave stretched craters, and those are a few per cent of all impacts. A slow stone thrown into sand is a different case: it ploughs through the sand and pushes it ahead, so its direction shows in the shape.

blocks.caption: A stony body 50 m across hits the Moon. Left, its path from the side; right, the crater and its ejecta from above. The shapes follow laboratory experiments in which projectiles were fired into sand and rock at up to 7 km a second (Gault and Wedekind, 1978), simplified; computer models of impacts show the same behaviour at higher speeds.
blocks.task: Find an impact below 20° at 10 km/s or faster that still leaves a round crater

blocks.caption: Messier and Messier A on the Moon's Sea of Fertility, two of the rare stretched craters. A body came in at a very low angle from the right, and the bright rays of debris fan out to the left, down its path.

blocks.text: The American astronomer Ralph Baldwin set out the full case in 1949 in *The Face of the Moon*. He showed that lunar craters, Earth's bomb and shell craters, and the few known meteorite craters all follow the same relationship between width and depth, while volcanic craters do not. Through the 1950s many astronomers came round to impacts. Many geologists did not, because there was still no way to tell an impact crater from a volcanic one by looking at the rocks.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: At 10 to 30 km a second an impactor stops almost at once and its energy spreads out as a shock wave from one point, like a buried explosion.
So impact craters are round unless the impact angle is very low, under about 15°.
The angle shows in the debris, which is thrown farther down the path the body was travelling.

blocks.text: Eugene Shoemaker, a young USGS geologist, found the evidence in the late 1950s. He had mapped the craters left by underground nuclear test explosions in Nevada, and when he mapped Meteor Crater he found the same structure: the rock layers in the rim were bent upward and folded back over themselves, so that near the crest the layers lay upside down, the order of a stack flipped like a page being turned (lesson 1's rule that lower is older, broken by the blast).

The deciding test was a mineral. Pure quartz, squeezed to pressures tens of thousands of times greater than the atmosphere's, rearranges its atoms into a denser form called **coesite**, first made in a laboratory in 1953. No volcano produces such a pressure near the surface. In 1960 Shoemaker, with Edward Chao and Beth Madsen, found coesite in the shocked sandstone of Meteor Crater. Within a year Shoemaker and Chao had found it at the Ries basin in Germany, a 24-kilometre circle around the town of Nördlingen long taken for a volcanic crater.

Other fingerprints of impact soon followed. **Shatter cones**, nested cones of fractured rock whose tips point back toward the source of the shock, were promoted as a marker by the American geologist Robert Dietz; they form only when a shock wave passes through rock. **Shocked quartz**, grains crossed by sets of microscopic planes where the crystal was deformed, turns up even in tiny fragments thrown far from a crater. Knowing what to look for, geologists have since confirmed about 190 impact structures on Earth, most of them worn down far below their original craters.

blocks.caption: A shatter cone. The fractures fan out downward from the tip, which pointed toward the shock that made them.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Shoemaker found the rim layers at Meteor Crater folded back on themselves, as at nuclear test craters.
Coesite, a form of quartz made only at enormous pressure, proved the impact origin of Meteor Crater and the Ries basin.
Shatter cones and shocked quartz are now used to identify impact structures even when the crater has worn away.

blocks.text: In 1961 President Kennedy committed the United States to landing on the Moon. Shoemaker, who had hoped to go himself until a health problem ruled him out, set up the USGS branch of astrogeology in Flagstaff, Arizona, and he and his colleagues taught the astronauts to work as field geologists. The crews, nearly all test pilots, spent hundreds of hours on field trips: to Meteor Crater, to the Grand Canyon to read layers, to Hawaii and Iceland for lava, and to the Sudbury impact structure in Canada for shatter cones. In 1967 the Survey even blasted a field of explosive craters into the cinders near Flagstaff, matching the sizes and spacing of the craters in photographs of Apollo 11's planned landing site, so the crews could rehearse.

blocks.caption: Apollo astronauts on a geology field trip on Earth, learning to describe and sample rocks.

blocks.text: Six crews landed between July 1969 and December 1972, and twelve men walked on the Moon. They brought back 382 kilograms of rock, pebbles, core tubes and soil, each sample photographed and described where it lay, the way a field geologist records a specimen. The last crew, Apollo 17, included Harrison Schmitt, a geologist with a doctorate from Harvard, the only scientist to walk on the Moon. Near a crater called Shorty he noticed orange soil, which turned out to be tiny beads of volcanic glass, sprayed out by fire fountains of lava 3.6 billion years ago.

blocks.caption: The six Apollo landings, in order from July 1969 to December 1972, and where each landed.

events.label: Apollo 11: Sea of Tranquility, a mare plain
Apollo 12: Ocean of Storms, beside Surveyor 3
Apollo 14: Fra Mauro, debris from the Imbrium basin
Apollo 15: Hadley Rille and the Apennine Mountains
Apollo 17: Taurus-Littrow valley, with a geologist

blocks.caption: Harrison Schmitt beside a split boulder at Taurus-Littrow on Apollo 17, December 1972.

blocks.text: The craters of the Moon were impact craters, and the samples now showed it too: the highland rocks are mostly **breccias**, rocks of broken and welded fragments, shattered and remelted again and again by impacts. The next three lessons are about what else the rocks revealed: how old the Moon's surfaces are, what its crust is made of, and where the Moon came from.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: USGS geologists trained the Apollo crews in field geology at Meteor Crater, the Grand Canyon, Hawaii and other sites.
Six Apollo landings (1969 to 1972) returned 382 kg of samples, each recorded where it was collected.
Most highland rocks are breccias, broken and re-welded by repeated impacts.

blocks.caption: Six questions on craters
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: What problem with his own impact idea could Gilbert not solve?
choices: Most impacts come in at a slant, and slanting hits were expected to make oval craters, yet the craters are round
The Moon's craters are far too small to have been made by impacts
Impacts would have knocked the Moon out of its orbit
items.why: A stone thrown at a slant into sand leaves an oval scoop. Gilbert could not explain why craters from mostly slanting impacts were round.

items.ask: Why does a body hitting the Moon at 20 km a second make a round crater even when it arrives at 45°?
choices: It stops almost at once, and its energy spreads out as a shock wave from one point, like a buried explosion
The Moon's weak gravity pulls every falling body into a vertical path
The Moon's soil is soft enough to flow back into any shape
items.why: At impact speeds the projectile delivers its energy at nearly a single point below the surface, so the hole is shaped like an explosion crater unless the body comes in very low.

items.ask: Why did Barringer's company never find a large mass of iron beneath Meteor Crater?
choices: Most of the iron body was vaporized or shattered in the impact
The iron had sunk deep into the Earth's mantle
The crater had been made by a steam explosion after all
items.why: The impactor's energy was enough to vaporize and scatter most of it. Only fragments and small grains of iron remain.

items.ask: Why was finding coesite at Meteor Crater decisive?
choices: Coesite forms only at pressures far beyond what volcanic activity produces near the surface
Coesite is a mineral found only inside meteorites
Coesite shows the rock was once soaked in water
items.why: Coesite is a dense form of quartz made at extreme pressure. At the surface only the shock of an impact can produce it.

items.ask: What is this, and what does it tell a geologist?
choices: A shatter cone, which forms only in rock struck by an impact's shock wave
A volcanic bomb, thrown out of an erupting vent
A fossil shell, flattened in mudstone
items.why: Shatter cones are nested, fanning fractures made by a shock wave. Finding them marks an impact structure even after the crater has eroded away.

items.ask: Messier and Messier A are stretched, and their debris fans out on one side. What does that show?
choices: The body came in at a very low, grazing angle
The body was moving unusually slowly
The craters are volcanic, not impact craters
items.why: Only impacts below about 15° leave stretched craters, and the debris is thrown down the path the body was travelling.

learned: Lunar craters are holes, not volcanic cones, and they are almost all round.
At impact speeds a body stops almost instantly and its energy spreads as a shock wave, so the crater is round unless the angle is very low.
Coesite, shatter cones and shocked quartz identify impact structures on Earth.
Geologists trained the Apollo crews, who returned 382 kg of samples from six landing sites.
